title: The Mahabharata
description: A dedicated, stage-by-stage study of the Mahabharata, the longest epic poem known: the Pandavas and Kauravas, the game of dice, exile, the Kurukshetra war and its aftermath, the great characters and their dilemmas, the epic's many stories-within-stories, its versions and performance traditions, and its enduring questions about dharma. Traditional narrative, belief, textual history and interpretation are clearly labelled.

structure.title: The eighteen Parvas of the Mahabharata
structure.intro: The Mahabharata, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa, contains roughly 100,000 verses in its longer versions. It is divided into 18 books (parvas). Scholars generally date its composition across several centuries, roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE. The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune produced a critical edition (1919–1966) by comparing manuscripts from across India.

sections.name: Adi Parva (The Beginning)
sections.summary: Origins of the Kuru family; births of the Pandavas and Kauravas; Bhishma's vow; the house of lac; Draupadi's svayamvara.

sections.name: Sabha Parva (The Assembly Hall)
sections.summary: The building of Indraprastha; the game of dice; Draupadi's humiliation in the assembly and her question; the Pandavas lose everything.

sections.name: Vana (Aranyaka) Parva (The Forest)
sections.summary: Twelve years of exile; many stories told in the forest, including Nala and Damayanti, Savitri and Satyavan, and the Yaksha's questions.

sections.name: Virata Parva
sections.summary: The thirteenth year spent in disguise at King Virata's court.

sections.name: Udyoga Parva (Preparations)
sections.summary: Efforts for peace, including Krishna's peace mission; both sides prepare for war.

sections.name: Bhishma Parva
sections.summary: The war begins at Kurukshetra; contains the Bhagavad Gita; Bhishma falls onto a bed of arrows.

sections.name: Drona Parva
sections.summary: Drona leads the Kauravas; Abhimanyu dies in the chakravyuha; Drona is killed.

sections.name: Karna Parva
sections.summary: Karna leads the Kaurava army and is killed by Arjuna.

sections.name: Shalya Parva
sections.summary: Shalya leads the Kauravas; the war ends with the duel between Bhima and Duryodhana.

sections.name: Sauptika Parva (The Sleeping Warriors)
sections.summary: Ashwatthama's night attack on the sleeping Pandava camp.

sections.name: Stri Parva (The Women)
sections.summary: The women of both sides grieve; Gandhari's lament and curse.

sections.name: Shanti Parva (Peace)
sections.summary: Bhishma, on his bed of arrows, teaches Yudhishthira about kingship, dharma and liberation.

sections.name: Anushasana Parva (Instructions)
sections.summary: Further teachings of Bhishma; his death.

sections.name: Ashvamedhika Parva
sections.summary: Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice to restore his kingdom.

sections.name: Ashramavasika Parva
sections.summary: Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti retire to the forest.

sections.name: Mausala Parva
sections.summary: The destruction of the Yadavas and the end of Krishna's earthly life.

sections.name: Mahaprasthanika Parva (The Great Journey)
sections.summary: The Pandavas and Draupadi set out on their final journey towards the Himalayas.

sections.name: Svargarohana Parva (Ascent to Heaven)
sections.summary: Yudhishthira's final test and arrival in heaven.

lessons.title: Five Brothers, Five Gifts
objectives: Name the five Pandava brothers
Describe one special quality of each
explanation: The Mahabharata is one of the longest stories ever told, from India. It is about a big family — two groups of cousins called the Pandavas and the Kauravas.

The five Pandava brothers each had a gift. Yudhishthira, the eldest, always tried to tell the truth. Bhima was the strongest. Arjuna was the finest archer. The twins, Nakula and Sahadeva, were handsome and wise.
Their friend and cousin Krishna often helped and guided them.

context.text: The Mahabharata is a traditional epic attributed to the sage Vyasa.

story.title: Arjuna Practises in the Dark
story.text: One night, the wind blew out the lamp while Arjuna was eating. Yet his hand still found his mouth in the dark. "If I can do this without seeing," Arjuna thought, "I can practise archery in the dark too." From that night, he practised every evening, until he became the finest archer of all.

lessons.title: What Do You See?
objectives: Retell the story of the bird's eye test
Explain what focus means
explanation: The princes had a wise teacher called Drona. One day, he put a wooden bird on a tree branch and asked each student, "What do you see?"
The other princes said, "I see the tree, the branch, the leaves, the bird, you, my brothers…" Drona told them not to shoot.
Arjuna said, "I see only the bird's eye." Drona smiled and said, "Shoot!" Arjuna's arrow hit the eye. Focusing on one thing helps us do it well.

context.text: The bird's eye test is a much-loved story from the Mahabharata tradition, often told to children.

story.title: The Wooden Bird
story.text: Drona placed a small wooden bird high in a tree. "Aim at its eye," he said. "But first tell me what you see." Yudhishthira said, "The tree, the sky, my brothers." Bhima said, "The bird and the leaves." Then Arjuna, very still, said, "Only the eye." Twang! went the bow. The arrow found its mark.

lessons.title: Yudhishthira and the Faithful Dog
objectives: Retell the story of Yudhishthira and the dog
Discuss loyalty and kindness to animals
explanation: At the very end of the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira walked a long, long journey up the Himalayas. A dog followed him all the way.
When a chariot came to take Yudhishthira to heaven, he was told the dog could not come. Yudhishthira said he would not leave his loyal friend behind.
Then the dog changed into Dharma, the god of righteousness — it had been a test! Yudhishthira had shown that he would not abandon a friend, even an animal.

context.text: This story comes from the Mahaprasthanika Parva, near the end of the Mahabharata.
In the tradition, Dharma is the deity of righteousness and Yudhishthira's father.

story.title: The Dog at the Mountain Top
story.text: Up and up the snowy mountain walked Yudhishthira, with a thin dog trotting beside him. At the top, a golden chariot appeared. "Come to heaven," said a voice, "but leave the dog." Yudhishthira shook his head. "He has walked with me all this way. I will not leave him." The dog glowed — and became Dharma himself, smiling.

lessons.title: Cousins and Rivals
objectives: Explain how the Pandavas and Kauravas are related
Describe how jealousy led to conflict
explanation: King Dhritarashtra, who was blind, had a hundred sons with Queen Gandhari, called the Kauravas; the eldest was Duryodhana. His brother Pandu's five sons were the Pandavas, raised by Queen Kunti (and Madri, mother of the twins).
The cousins grew up together in Hastinapura, taught by Drona and protected by their great-uncle Bhishma, who had vowed never to marry or claim the throne.

Duryodhana grew jealous of the Pandavas' skills and popularity. In one story, he tried to harm them in a house made of lac (a material that burns easily), but they escaped through a secret tunnel, warned by their wise uncle Vidura.

context.text: These events are told in the Adi Parva.
Some readers see Duryodhana purely as a villain; others note he felt the throne was rightfully his father's line, and tellings vary in sympathy.

lessons.title: A Game That Went Too Far
objectives: Retell the game of dice
Discuss gambling, fairness and Draupadi's courage
explanation: The Pandavas built a beautiful city, Indraprastha. Duryodhana, jealous, invited Yudhishthira to a game of dice. His uncle Shakuni, a cunning player, threw the dice for him.
Yudhishthira kept betting and losing — his wealth, his kingdom, his brothers, himself and finally even Draupadi, the Pandavas' wife. It was a terrible mistake.

Draupadi was dragged into the assembly and insulted. She bravely asked the elders a question no one could answer: if Yudhishthira had already lost himself, did he have the right to bet her? In the end, the Pandavas were sent into exile for thirteen years.

context.text: The game of dice is the turning point of the Sabha Parva.
In many tellings, Krishna miraculously protects Draupadi's honour when Dushasana tries to pull off her sari; devotees see this as divine protection.
Draupadi's question in the assembly is discussed by scholars as a profound challenge about law, rights and justice.

story.title: Draupadi's Question
story.text: In the great hall, everyone fell silent as Draupadi stood before the elders. "Tell me," she said, "when my husband had already lost himself, whose right was it to wager me?" Bhishma bowed his head. Drona looked away. Only Vikarna, one of the Kauravas, spoke up for her. Her question echoed through the hall — and through history.

lessons.title: The Yaksha's Questions
objectives: Retell the story of the Yaksha's questions
Discuss the wisdom in Yudhishthira's answers
explanation: During their exile, the thirsty Pandavas found a lake. A voice — a yaksha (a nature spirit) — warned that whoever drank before answering its questions would fall. Four brothers ignored the warning, drank, and fell lifeless.

Yudhishthira came and agreed to answer. The yaksha asked many riddles: "What is faster than the wind?" — "The mind." "What is the greatest wonder?" — "That every day people see others die, yet live as if they never will."
Pleased, the yaksha offered to bring back one brother. Yudhishthira chose Nakula, son of Madri, so that both mothers would have a living son. The yaksha, revealed as Dharma, restored all four.

context.text: The Yaksha Prashna (Yaksha's questions) is in the Vana Parva.
Readers often see Yudhishthira's choice of Nakula as an example of fairness beyond self-interest.

"Kunti has a living son — me," Yudhishthira explained. "Madri should have one too." The yaksha smiled and restored all four brothers.

lessons.title: Five Villages for Peace
objectives: Describe attempts to avoid war
Discuss why peace efforts failed
explanation: In the thirteenth year, the Pandavas hid in disguise at King Virata's court: Yudhishthira as a dice-playing courtier, Bhima as a cook, Arjuna as a dance teacher, Draupadi as a maid.
After the exile, they asked for their kingdom back. Duryodhana refused. Krishna went to Hastinapura on a peace mission and finally asked for only five villages for the five brothers.

Duryodhana declared he would not give even as much land as the point of a needle. War became certain. Leaders chose sides; Krishna offered his army to one side and himself, unarmed, to the other. Arjuna chose Krishna; Duryodhana chose the army.

context.text: Krishna's peace mission is told in the Udyoga Parva.
Readers debate whether war could have been avoided and who bears responsibility.

lessons.title: The Great War
objectives: Sequence the main events of the war
Discuss courage and tragedy in the war
explanation: The armies met at Kurukshetra. Before the battle, Arjuna saw his relatives and teachers on the other side and refused to fight. Krishna's guidance to him is the Bhagavad Gita.

The war lasted eighteen days. Bhishma, the great-uncle, fought for the Kauravas and fell on a bed of arrows. Arjuna's young son Abhimanyu knew how to enter the chakravyuha (a circular battle formation) but not how to leave it; he fought bravely and was killed.
Drona and Karna fell, and at last Bhima defeated Duryodhana. The Pandavas won — but almost everyone was dead. The epic shows war's terrible cost.

context.text: The war is described across the Bhishma, Drona, Karna and Shalya Parvas.
Many readers see the Mahabharata as deeply critical of war, showing victory without joy.
Kurukshetra is a real place in Haryana; whether a historical battle lies behind the epic is debated, and no archaeological evidence confirms the war as described.

story.title: Abhimanyu's Courage
story.text: Abhimanyu had learned, as a baby in his mother's womb, how to break into the chakravyuha — but he never heard how to break out. When no one else could stop the formation, the sixteen-year-old rode in alone. He fought with astonishing courage until he was surrounded and fell. His story is told with both admiration and grief.

lessons.title: Karna's Choices
objectives: Retell Karna's story
Analyse questions of identity, loyalty and fairness it raises
explanation: Karna was secretly Kunti's first son, born before her marriage and set afloat in a river. He was raised by a charioteer's family and faced insults because of his birth, even though he was a superb archer.

When others mocked him, Duryodhana made him a king, and Karna became his loyal friend. Before the war, Kunti and Krishna told Karna the truth and asked him to join the Pandavas, his brothers. He refused to betray Duryodhana, though he promised Kunti he would not kill any Pandava except Arjuna.

Karna was famous for generosity — he gave away his protective armour and earrings when asked. Readers see him as a tragic hero. Stories like Karna's and Ekalavya's (a tribal archer denied training) raise questions about birth, status and fairness that people still debate.

context.text: Karna's story spans several parvas; the episode of giving away his armour is especially celebrated.
Many modern readers and writers, such as Shivaji Sawant in the Marathi novel "Mrityunjay", explore Karna's perspective and the injustice of caste-based exclusion.

lessons.title: The Grief of the Mothers
objectives: Describe the aftermath of the war
Discuss grief, responsibility and learning from loss
explanation: After the war, the women of both sides came to the battlefield to mourn. Gandhari, mother of the hundred Kauravas, wept for all her sons. In her grief, she blamed Krishna for not preventing the war and cursed his clan.
Bhishma, still lying on his bed of arrows, taught Yudhishthira about good rule, justice and dharma (the Shanti and Anushasana Parvas). Yudhishthira ruled, but felt deep sorrow at the cost of victory.
Years later, the Pandavas and Draupadi set out on a final journey towards the Himalayas — the ending with Yudhishthira and the faithful dog.

context.text: Gandhari's lament is in the Stri Parva; Bhishma's teachings fill the Shanti and Anushasana Parvas.
The Stri Parva is often read as one of literature's earliest powerful portrayals of war's cost from women's perspective.

lessons.title: Ashwatthama Is Dead
objectives: Analyse the "half-truth" episode as a moral dilemma
Explain the idea that dharma is subtle
explanation: The Mahabharata repeatedly says "dharma is subtle" (sukshma) — knowing the right action is often difficult.

To defeat their teacher Drona, the Pandavas needed him to stop fighting. Bhima killed an elephant named Ashwatthama — the same name as Drona's son. Yudhishthira, known never to lie, told Drona "Ashwatthama is dead," adding quietly "…the elephant." Drona, hearing only the first part, laid down his weapons. In the story, Yudhishthira's chariot, which had always floated above the ground, touched the earth.
Episodes like this — and Krishna's battlefield strategies — show the epic questioning whether good ends justify troubling means.

context.text: The half-truth episode is told in the Drona Parva.
Commentators and philosophers, including in modern works like Gurcharan Das's "The Difficulty of Being Good", discuss these episodes as explorations of moral complexity.

lessons.title: Savitri and the Lord of Death
objectives: Retell embedded stories like Savitri and Nala–Damayanti
Explain how stories-within-stories work in the epic
explanation: The Mahabharata contains many smaller stories (upakhyanas) told by sages to the Pandavas. They comfort, teach or illustrate ideas.

Savitri chose to marry Satyavan, knowing he was destined to die within a year. When Yama, the lord of death, came for him, she followed Yama, arguing so wisely and persistently that he granted her wishes — and through a clever wish, Satyavan's life was restored.

Nala and Damayanti's story tells of love, loss through gambling and reunion — a mirror of Yudhishthira's own situation. The epic itself is framed as a story told by Vaishampayana, a pupil of Vyasa, to King Janamejaya.

context.text: Savitri's story and Nala–Damayanti are upakhyanas in the Vana Parva; Vat Savitri is observed by many married women in parts of India.
Modern readers see Savitri both as a model of devotion and as a figure of intelligence and agency who outwits death.

lessons.title: Draupadi's Voice
objectives: Analyse Draupadi as a central character
Discuss how the epic explores gender and justice
explanation: Draupadi is one of the epic's strongest voices. Born from fire, she is intelligent, outspoken and fierce in demanding justice for the wrong done to her in the assembly hall.
Her question to the elders — whether a man who had lost himself could wager his wife — exposes failures of law and of the powerful, who stayed silent.

Other women, like Kunti, Gandhari and Amba (who sought revenge on Bhishma and was reborn as Shikhandi), shape the story too. Modern writers such as Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni ("The Palace of Illusions") and Mahasweta Devi ("Draupadi") have retold the epic from women's and marginalised perspectives.

context.text: Draupadi is revered as a goddess in some communities, such as in the Draupadi Amman tradition of Tamil Nadu.
Scholars read Draupadi's question as a profound legal and ethical challenge; feminist readings highlight her agency and the silence of powerful men.

lessons.title: From Jaya to the Critical Edition
objectives: Explain how the Mahabharata grew over time
Describe the BORI Critical Edition and its significance
explanation: The epic itself mentions earlier, shorter forms — "Jaya" and "Bharata" — that grew into the Mahabharata. Scholars think it was composed and expanded over several centuries, roughly 400 BCE to 400 CE, with many contributors in an oral and then written tradition, though tradition attributes it to Vyasa.

Manuscripts from different regions differ greatly. From 1919 to 1966, scholars at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune, led by V. S. Sukthankar, compared hundreds of manuscripts to produce a critical edition — noticeably shorter than popular printed versions — recording thousands of variant passages in footnotes and appendices.

Regional versions and performance traditions — like Pandavani in Chhattisgarh (made famous by Teejan Bai), the Tamil Villi Bharatam, and Kannada and Telugu Mahabharatas — show the epic as a living, multilingual tradition.

context.text: The BORI Critical Edition was completed in 1966 in Pune; Teejan Bai, a Pandavani performer, received the Padma Vibhushan in 2019.
Many Hindus regard the Mahabharata as itihasa ("thus it happened") and Vyasa as its divinely inspired author.
Scholars debate the stages of composition and how to date them.

story.title: Fifty Years of Comparison
story.text: For nearly fifty years, scholars in Pune laid out manuscripts from Kashmir to Kerala — on palm leaves, birch bark and paper — comparing verse by verse. Where versions differed, they recorded every variant. The result is not "the one true text" but a map of how an epic travelled and grew across India.

lessons.title: The Duties of a King
objectives: Analyse ideas of rajadharma in the Shanti Parva
Evaluate their relevance to modern governance and ethics
explanation: In the Shanti Parva, Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira rajadharma — the duties of a ruler: protecting the people, ensuring justice, caring for the weak, and governing with counsel. A king, he says, exists for the welfare of the people.
Yudhishthira, sickened by the war, wants to renounce the throne and become an ascetic. The epic stages a debate: is withdrawal from the world or active responsibility the higher path?

Vidura Niti (in the Udyoga Parva) offers practical wisdom on ethics and leadership. Thinkers from Gandhi to modern philosophers and economists (such as Amartya Sen, discussing nyaya and niti) have drawn on the epic's ideas about justice.

context.text: The teachings of the Shanti Parva are presented as Bhishma's instruction to Yudhishthira.
Scholars interpret the epic's political thought variously; Amartya Sen's "The Idea of Justice" (2009) contrasts niti (rules) and nyaya (realised justice) drawing on Indian traditions.

Running away is not peace." Their debate — between escape and responsibility — is one of the epic's deepest conversations.
